title: Wilt thou be made whole (John 5:1–9)
hookLine: a man ill thirty-eight years is asked if he wants to be healed
tomorrow: I am the bread of life

lines: A CROWD WAITING FOR THE WATER.
cards: Near the sheep gate in Jerusalem there's a pool with five porches, covered walkways around the water. The Douay-Rheims calls it Probatica, from the Greek for sheep; most Bibles know it as Bethesda.
The porches are full of the blind, the lame, the withered, lying on mats, waiting. People said that now and then the water was stirred, and the first one in would be healed.
One man has been lying there thirty-eight years under his illness, John tells us. Today Jesus finds him and asks a question that sounds almost rude.

teach.b: Jesus knows he has been that way a long time, and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Wilt thou be made whole?" Do you want to get well? On the surface it's absurd.
Of course he does. But listen: he doesn't say yes.
"Sir, I have no man, when the water is troubled, to put me into the pond." Someone always gets there first. It's an explanation, and a lonely one.
After thirty-eight years, the story he tells about his life has become: it's never going to be me. Jesus doesn't argue with the story, and he doesn't carry him to the water.
He says: "Arise, take up thy bed, and walk." And immediately the man is made whole, picks up his mat, and walks.

The question matters because a man ill for thirty-eight years has a whole life built around it: a place to lie, a way of asking, a way of being seen. Being made whole means standing up into a life he doesn't know yet.
The Church teaches that God respects our freedom, even in healing; grace is offered, not forced. Two honest notes.
Some old manuscripts include a verse about an angel stirring the water; many of the earliest leave it out, and modern Catholic Bibles often put it in a footnote.

teach.h: A REAL POOL BY SAINT ANNE'S.
teach.b: And the pool is real: near the Church of Saint Anne in Jerusalem, archaeologists found two large pools with a wall between them, which some think explains the five porches.

how: Catholics hear the healing at the pool on a weekday of the fourth week of Lent, and pilgrims to Jerusalem visit the excavated pools beside the Church of Saint Anne.

o: have you confessed what you've done?
do you truly want to be healed?

games.q: you've been ill thirty-eight years, lying by a healing pool. a stranger asks: do you want to be made whole? what do you say?
o: sir, I have no one to put me in the water.
games.why: he gives his reason: someone always gets there first. Jesus doesn't argue. he says: arise, take up thy bed, and walk.

practice: Think of one place where you've been stuck a long time, a habit, a hurt, a fear, a relationship gone flat, and hear the question gently: do you want to be made whole?
Notice your first answer, a yes or a reason like his, and just hear it without judging. If you pray, give God your honest answer; if not, just let yourself know what it is.

wordCard.voice: Wilt thou be made whole. Jesus's question to a man ill for thirty-eight years by the pool of Bethesda, before he told him to rise and walk. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: whole, healthy, sound (John 5:6). The root of the English word hygiene.

carryVoice: Your line: wilt thou be made whole. A gentle question, and then: arise. That's day five hundred two.
